Clear Protocols for Personal Data Breach Notification
The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes
place, the Data Fiduciary must inform all affected individuals without delay. The message must be in plain
language and must explain what happened, the possible impact and the steps taken to address the issue.
It must also include contact details for help.

Transparency and Accountability Measures
The Rules require every Data Fiduciary to display clear contact information for queries related to personal
data. This may be the contact of a designated officer or a Data Protection Officer. Significant Data
Fiduciaries face stronger duties. They must conduct independent audits and carry out impact assessments.
They must also follow stricter checks while using new or sensitive technologies. In some cases, they must
follow government directions on restricted categories of data, including local storage where needed.

Strengthening Rights of Data Principals
The Rules reinforce the rights already provided under the Act. Individuals can ask to access their personal
data or seek corrections and updates. They may also request the removal of data in certain situations.
They can choose someone else to exercise these rights on their behalf. Data Fiduciaries must respond to
such requests within ninety days.

• Data Fiduciary: An entity that decides why and how personal data is processed, either alone
or with others.

• Data Principal: The individual to whom the personal data relates. In the case of a child, this
includes a parent or lawful guardian. For a person with a disability who cannot act
independently, this includes the lawful guardian acting on their behalf.

• Data Processor: Any entity that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.

• Consent Manager: An entity that provides a single, transparent and interoperable platform
through which a Data Principal may give, manage, review or withdraw consent.

• Appellate Tribunal: The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), which
hears appeals against decisions of the Data Protection Board.
Penalties Under the DPDP Act, 2023
The DPDP Act imposes substantial financial penalties for non-compliance by Data Fiduciaries. The
highest penalty up to ₹250 crore applies to failure of a Data Fiduciary to maintain reasonable security
safeguards. Not notifying the Board or affected individuals of a personal data breach as well as
violations of obligations relating to children can each attract penalties of up to ₹200 crore. Any other
violation of the Act or Rules by a Data Fiduciary may attract penalties up to ₹50 crore.

question: Who must be told about a personal data breach, and how, under the Rules?
expected_answer: Each affected Data Principal, in a concise, clear and plain manner and without delay, through her user account or any communication mode she registered (rule 7(1)).
answer:
The Rules require the Data Fiduciary to inform every affected Data Principal — without delay and in plain, concise language—through the user’s account or any communication mode the principal has registered, providing a description of the breach, likely consequences, mitigation measures, safety steps the principal can take, and contact details of a person who can respond to queries【1†L1-L5】.  
The Fiduciary must also notify the Board, initially with a brief description and then, within 72 hours (or a longer period if approved), with detailed information, the facts leading to the breach and the measures taken or proposed to mitigate risk【1†L6-L9】.

People may request corrections to personal data that is inaccurate or incomplete.

Right to Update Personal Data
Citizens can ask for changes when their details have altered, such as a new address or updated contact
number.

Right to Erase Personal Data
Individuals may request the removal of personal data in certain situations. The Data Fiduciary must
consider and act on this request within the permitted time.

Right to Nominate Another Person
Every individual can appoint someone to exercise their data rights on their behalf. This is helpful in cases
of illness or other limitations.

Mandatory Response within Ninety Days
Data Fiduciaries are required to address all requests related to access, correction, updating or erasure
within a maximum of ninety days, ensuring timely action and accountability.

If a breach takes place, citizens must be informed at the earliest. The message must explain what

designated officer or a Data Protection Officer.

When a child’s personal data is involved, verifiable consent from a parent or guardian is required. This
consent is needed unless the processing relates to essential services such as healthcare, education or real-time safety.

People may request corrections to personal data that is inaccurate or incomplete.

Right to Update Personal Data
Citizens can ask for changes when their details have altered, such as a new address or updated contact
number.

Right to Erase Personal Data
Individuals may request the removal of personal data in certain situations. The Data Fiduciary must
consider and act on this request within the permitted time.

Right to Nominate Another Person
Every individual can appoint someone to exercise their data rights on their behalf. This is helpful in cases
of illness or other limitations.

Mandatory Response within Ninety Days
Data Fiduciaries are required to address all requests related to access, correction, updating or erasure
within a maximum of ninety days, ensuring timely action and accountability.

Protection During Personal Data Breaches
If a breach takes place, citizens must be informed at the earliest. The message must explain what
happened and what steps they can take. This helps people act quickly to reduce harm.

Clear Contact for Queries and Complaints
Data Fiduciaries must provide a point of contact for questions relating to personal data. This may be a
designated officer or a Data Protection Officer.
Special Protection for Children
When a child’s personal data is involved, verifiable consent from a parent or guardian is required. This
consent is needed unless the processing relates to essential services such as healthcare, education or real-time safety.

question: What does the Act require on a personal data breach, and what exactly do the Rules add about timing and content?
expected_answer: Act s.8(6): the Data Fiduciary must intimate the Board and each affected Data Principal in the prescribed form and manner. Rules r.7: affected persons without delay with description, consequences, measures, safety steps and contact; Board without delay, then detailed information within seventy-two hours.
answer:
The Act obliges a Data Fiduciary to give an intimation of a personal‑data breach to the Data Protection Board, which may then direct urgent remedial measures and may inquire and impose penalties【3】.  

The Rules specify that the fiduciary must inform each affected Data Principal “without delay” in plain language, describing the breach, its likely impact, mitigation steps, safety measures for the principal and a contact for queries【1】.  It must also notify the Board “without delay” with a description of the breach and, within 72 hours of becoming aware (or a longer period the Board permits), provide detailed updated information, the facts leading to the breach and the measures taken or proposed to mitigate risk【1】.

contexts:
Clear Protocols for Personal Data Breach Notification
The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes
place, the Data Fiduciary must inform all affected individuals without delay. The message must be in plain
language and must explain what happened, the possible impact and the steps taken to address the issue.
It must also include contact details for help.

Transparency and Accountability Measures
The Rules require every Data Fiduciary to display clear contact information for queries related to personal
data. This may be the contact of a designated officer or a Data Protection Officer. Significant Data
Fiduciaries face stronger duties. They must conduct independent audits and carry out impact assessments.
They must also follow stricter checks while using new or sensitive technologies. In some cases, they must
follow government directions on restricted categories of data, including local storage where needed.

Strengthening Rights of Data Principals
The Rules reinforce the rights already provided under the Act. Individuals can ask to access their personal
data or seek corrections and updates. They may also request the removal of data in certain situations.
They can choose someone else to exercise these rights on their behalf. Data Fiduciaries must respond to
such requests within ninety days.

Digital-First Data Protection Board

namely:—
(a) on receipt of an intimation of personal data breach under sub-section (6) of

personal data breach, and to inquire into such personal data breach and impose

(b) on a complaint made by a Data Principal in respect of a personal data breach

reference made to it by the Central Government or a State Government, or in compliance
of the directions of any court, to inquire into such breach and impose penalty as

People may request corrections to personal data that is inaccurate or incomplete.

Right to Update Personal Data
Citizens can ask for changes when their details have altered, such as a new address or updated contact
number.

Right to Erase Personal Data
Individuals may request the removal of personal data in certain situations. The Data Fiduciary must
consider and act on this request within the permitted time.

Right to Nominate Another Person
Every individual can appoint someone to exercise their data rights on their behalf. This is helpful in cases
of illness or other limitations.

Mandatory Response within Ninety Days
Data Fiduciaries are required to address all requests related to access, correction, updating or erasure
within a maximum of ninety days, ensuring timely action and accountability.

Protection During Personal Data Breaches
If a breach takes place, citizens must be informed at the earliest. The message must explain what
happened and what steps they can take. This helps people act quickly to reduce harm.

Clear Contact for Queries and Complaints
Data Fiduciaries must provide a point of contact for questions relating to personal data. This may be a
designated officer or a Data Protection Officer.
Special Protection for Children
When a child’s personal data is involved, verifiable consent from a parent or guardian is required. This
consent is needed unless the processing relates to essential services such as healthcare, education or real-time safety.

question: What penalty applies if a Data Fiduciary fails to notify the Board or affected persons of a breach, and what deadline does the rule set for the Board?
expected_answer: Up to two hundred crore rupees (Act Schedule, item 2); the Board must be told without delay and then within seventy-two hours with details (Rules r.7(2)).
answer: The DPDP Act provides that a Data Fiduciary who does not notify the Board or the affected Data Principals of a personal data breach can be penalised up to ₹200 crore [2]. The Rules do not specify a deadline that the Board must meet in this context; they only set a 72‑hour reporting window for the Fiduciary to inform the Board after becoming aware of the breach [1].

contexts:
• Data Fiduciary: An entity that decides why and how personal data is processed, either alone
or with others.

• Data Principal: The individual to whom the personal data relates. In the case of a child, this
includes a parent or lawful guardian. For a person with a disability who cannot act
independently, this includes the lawful guardian acting on their behalf.

• Data Processor: Any entity that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.

• Consent Manager: An entity that provides a single, transparent and interoperable platform
through which a Data Principal may give, manage, review or withdraw consent.

• Appellate Tribunal: The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), which
hears appeals against decisions of the Data Protection Board.
Penalties Under the DPDP Act, 2023
The DPDP Act imposes substantial financial penalties for non-compliance by Data Fiduciaries. The
highest penalty up to ₹250 crore applies to failure of a Data Fiduciary to maintain reasonable security
safeguards. Not notifying the Board or affected individuals of a personal data breach as well as
violations of obligations relating to children can each attract penalties of up to ₹200 crore. Any other
violation of the Act or Rules by a Data Fiduciary may attract penalties up to ₹50 crore.
The Act places clear responsibilities on Data Fiduciaries to keep personal data safe and to stay accountable

Clear Protocols for Personal Data Breach Notification
The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes
place, the Data Fiduciary must inform all affected individuals without delay. The message must be in plain
language and must explain what happened, the possible impact and the steps taken to address the issue.
It must also include contact details for help.

Transparency and Accountability Measures
The Rules require every Data Fiduciary to display clear contact information for queries related to personal
data. This may be the contact of a designated officer or a Data Protection Officer. Significant Data
Fiduciaries face stronger duties. They must conduct independent audits and carry out impact assessments.
They must also follow stricter checks while using new or sensitive technologies. In some cases, they must
follow government directions on restricted categories of data, including local storage where needed.

Strengthening Rights of Data Principals
The Rules reinforce the rights already provided under the Act. Individuals can ask to access their personal
data or seek corrections and updates. They may also request the removal of data in certain situations.
They can choose someone else to exercise these rights on their behalf. Data Fiduciaries must respond to
such requests within ninety days.

question: When must a Data Fiduciary erase personal data, and what must it do before erasing under the Third Schedule time periods?
expected_answer: Act s.8(7): erase when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served, unless law requires retention. Rules r.8(2): inform the Data Principal at least forty-eight hours before the erasure period completes.
answer:
A Data Fiduciary must erase personal data when the purpose for which it was collected is no longer being served, unless retention is required by law or for the time‑period specified in the Third Schedule [3][1].  
If the erasure is to occur after a Third‑Schedule time period, the fiduciary must notify the Data Principal at least forty‑eight hours before the end of that period that the data will be erased, unless the principal logs in or otherwise contacts the fiduciary to continue the purpose or exercise any right [1].

question: How does an appeal against a Board order work under the Act and the Rules?
expected_answer: Act s.29: appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days. Rules r.22: filed digitally, with a fee payable digitally using UPI or another RBI-authorised system.
answer: An appeal against an order or direction of the Board must be filed within 60 days of receipt of that order, in the form and manner prescribed and with the fee prescribed (or waived) by the Board [1][2]. The appeal is made to the Appellate Tribunal, which may admit a late appeal if it is satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay [1]. Under the 2025 Rules the appeal must be filed in digital form, the fee is to be paid digitally (e.g., via UPI), and the Tribunal is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure but may set its own procedure guided by natural‑justice principles [4]. The Tribunal may hear the appeal digitally, issue orders and, if needed, have those orders executed as a civil‑court decree [5].
disclaimer: This is information from the official DPDP documents, not legal advice.

question: How is a Consent Manager registered, and which conditions must it meet?
expected_answer: Act s.6(9): registered with the Board. Rules r.4 and First Schedule Part A: apply to the Board; must be an Indian company with net worth not less than two crore rupees, among other conditions.
answer:
A company that wishes to act as a Consent Manager must apply to the Board, furnishing the particulars and documents prescribed on the Board’s website; the Board then may inquire into the applicant’s compliance, and if satisfied it registers the applicant and publishes its details, otherwise it rejects the application with reasons [1].  
To be eligible for registration, the applicant must be an Indian‑incorporated company that has sufficient technical, operational and financial capacity; a sound financial condition and management character; a net‑worth of at least ₹2 crore; adequate business volume, capital structure and earnings prospects; directors and senior managers of proven fairness and integrity; constitutional provisions ensuring adherence to conflict‑of‑interest obligations; operations that serve Data Principals’ interests; and an independent certification that its interoperable consent platform meets the Board’s data‑protection standards [5].

question: What must a Data Fiduciary do before processing a child's personal data, and how is the parent's identity checked?
expected_answer: Act s.9(1): obtain verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian. Rules r.10: use appropriate technical and organisational measures and due diligence to check the parent is an identifiable adult.
answer: A Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable consent from the child’s parent or lawful guardian before any processing of the child’s personal data [2][4]. To verify the parent’s identity, the fiduciary must confirm that the person identifying as the parent is an identifiable adult by checking either (a) reliable identity and age details already held by the fiduciary, or (b) identity and age details (or a virtual token) provided voluntarily or issued by an authorised entity such as a Digital Locker service provider [4][1].

The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes

The Rules require every Data Fiduciary to display clear contact information for queries related to personal
data. This may be the contact of a designated officer or a Data Protection Officer. Significant Data

People may request corrections to personal data that is inaccurate or incomplete.

Right to Update Personal Data
Citizens can ask for changes when their details have altered, such as a new address or updated contact
number.

Right to Erase Personal Data
Individuals may request the removal of personal data in certain situations. The Data Fiduciary must
consider and act on this request within the permitted time.

Right to Nominate Another Person
Every individual can appoint someone to exercise their data rights on their behalf. This is helpful in cases

Mandatory Response within Ninety Days
Data Fiduciaries are required to address all requests related to access, correction, updating or erasure
within a maximum of ninety days, ensuring timely action and accountability.

Protection During Personal Data Breaches
If a breach takes place, citizens must be informed at the earliest. The message must explain what
happened and what steps they can take. This helps people act quickly to reduce harm.

Data Fiduciaries must provide a point of contact for questions relating to personal data. This may be a
designated officer or a Data Protection Officer.

consent is needed unless the processing relates to essential services such as healthcare, education or real-time safety.

The Government of India notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, 2025 on 14

their views. In total, 6,915 inputs were received during the consultation process. These contributions
played a key role in shaping the final Rules.1
With the notification of the Rules, India now has a practical and innovation-friendly system for data
protection. It supports ease of understanding, encourages compliance and strengthens trust in the
country’s growing digital ecosystem.

Overview of the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 give full effect to the DPDP Act, 2023. They build a clear
and practical system to protect personal data in a fast-expanding digital environment. The Rules focus on
the rights of citizens and on responsible data use by organisations. The Rules aim to curb unauthorized
commercial use of data, reduce digital harms and create a safe space for innovation. They will also help
India maintain a strong and trusted digital economy.
In carrying this vision forward, the Rules outline several core provisions that follow:

Phased and Practical Implementation
The Rules introduce an eighteen-month period for phased compliance. This gives organisations enough
time to adjust their systems and adopt responsible data practices. Every Data Fiduciary must issue a
separate consent notice that is clear and easy to understand. The notice must explain the specific purpose
for which personal data is collected and used. Consent Managers, who help people manage their
permissions, must be companies based in India.

The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes

Clear Protocols for Personal Data Breach Notification
The Rules set out a simple and timely process for reporting personal data breaches. When a breach takes
place, the Data Fiduciary must inform all affected individuals without delay. The message must be in plain
language and must explain what happened, the possible impact and the steps taken to address the issue.
It must also include contact details for help.

Transparency and Accountability Measures
The Rules require every Data Fiduciary to display clear contact information for queries related to personal
data. This may be the contact of a designated officer or a Data Protection Officer. Significant Data
Fiduciaries face stronger duties. They must conduct independent audits and carry out impact assessments.
They must also follow stricter checks while using new or sensitive technologies. In some cases, they must
follow government directions on restricted categories of data, including local storage where needed.

Strengthening Rights of Data Principals
The Rules reinforce the rights already provided under the Act. Individuals can ask to access their personal
data or seek corrections and updates. They may also request the removal of data in certain situations.
They can choose someone else to exercise these rights on their behalf. Data Fiduciaries must respond to
such requests within ninety days.
